CASE REPORT
Stiff-Person Syndrome
Persistent Elevation of Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase Antibodies Despite Successful
Treatment With Rituximab
Eugene A. Bacorro, MD, and Rodney Tehrani, MD
Abstract: Stiff-person syndrome is a rare neurologic disorder characterized
by ﬂuctuating and progressive stiffness of axial and limb musculature. The
high prevalence of autoantibodies and associated autoimmune diseases in
patients with stiff person syndrome suggests that it may have an autoimmune
etiology. We report a case of a 62-year-old man with diabetes who developed
progressive stiffness of the hips and legs and elevated levels of antibody to
glutamic acid decarboxylase. He had a partial response to both baclofen and
diazepam, but could not tolerate the treatment because of somnolence. He
eventually received 2 infusions of rituximab 1000 mg a week apart. The
baclofen was discontinued and the diazepam was tapered. However, 6
months after the rituximab treatment, despite continued clinical improvement
the patient had persistently elevated titers of antibody to glutamic acid
decarboxylase. We postulate that rituximab was associated with clinical
improvement through mechanisms other than antibody depletion.
Key Words: stiff-person syndrome, rituximab, case report
(J Clin Rheumatol 2010;16: 237–239)
S
tiff person syndrome (SPS) or stiff-man syndrome, is a rare
neurologic disorder characterized by ﬂuctuating and progressive
stiffness of axial and limb musculature, with painful spasms precip-
itated by movements or emotional stimuli.
1 The frequent ﬁnding of
elevated glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) autoantibodies in SPS
suggests that it may be an autoimmune disease even though the
pathogenic role of the antibodies is still unclear.
2 SPS is also often
associated with other autoimmune disorders like diabetes, thyroid-
itis, myasthenia gravis, pernicious anemia, and vitiligo. The treat-
ment of SPS is directed at pharmacologic enhancement of
/H9253-ami-
nobutyric acid (GABA) neurotransmission and suppression or
removal of GAD autoantibodies.
3 Medications that are generally
used to treat SPS include benzodiazepines, baclofen, as well as
antiepileptic drugs like valproate, levetiracetam, and gabapentin. 3,4
Immunomodulation, including corticosteroids, plasmapheresis, 5 in-
travenous immunoglobulin,6 and B lymphocyte depletion with anti-
CD20 (rituximab)7 have also been used successfully in the treatment
of SPS, with a corresponding decline in the level of antibodies to
glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD). We report the case of a
patient with SPS, who had good clinical response to rituximab
treatment in spite of persistently elevated anti-GAD levels.
CASE REPORT
A 62-year-old African-American man was referred to the
rheumatology clinic because of lower extremity weakness and
stiffness. For the past year, he has been complaining of shooting
pains and numbness of his legs with associated weakness, and was
diagnosed elsewhere as having a lumbar radiculopathy. He subse-
quently developed progressive stiffness of the hips and legs, along
with experiencing difﬁculty in getting out of a chair or turning over
in bed. The stiffness was worsened by stressful events. He had no
upper extremity pain, weakness, or stiffness. There was no joint pain
or swelling. There was no history of fevers, chills, weight loss,
photosensitive rash, Raynaud phenomenon, oral sores, dry eyes or
mouth, chest pains, dyspnea, gastrointestinal or genitourinary com-

plaints. Previous evaluation revealed elevated antinuclear antibody
(ANA) and anti-SSA/SSB titers, mildly elevated creatine kinase
levels, normal aldolase level, and an elevated thyroid stimulating
hormone level of 6.8 mIU/L (N: 0.5– 4.7). A spinal magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) revealed mild to moderate cervical and
lumbar stenosis. An electromyography performed on the right lower
extremity and lumbar paraspinal muscles was normal, even though
the patient was unable to completely relax the paraspinal muscles. A
lower extremity MRI showed normal musculature, and atrophic
changes but no inﬂammation or inclusion bodies were present in a
right thigh biopsy. He was started on a trial of prednisone 40 mg/d
with some improvement manifested as being able to get out of bed
by himself. He was also begun on levothyroxin 0.75 mg daily as a
result of which the thyroid stimulating hormone subsequently nor-
malized. His prednisone was slowly tapered to 10 mg/day. However,
he continued to have stiffness and rigidity of his legs, and fell twice
as a result of loss of balance. He was then started on 10 mg of
baclofen 3 times a day with only minimal improvement, and sub-
sequently was referred to the rheumatology clinic.
The patient had been diagnosed with diabetes 2 years ago,
which was controlled by subcutaneously administrating insulin
glargine 15 mg daily. He also suffered from hypertension. He had
benign prostatic hypertrophy and was treated by post-transurethral
resection of the prostate with multiple biopsies, which were all
negative for malignancy. He had undergone a colonoscopy 4 years
ago, which was normal. He had been smoking a pack of cigarettes
per day for 20 years but had stopped doing so from the past 20 years
or more. He denied alcohol intake or the use of illicit drugs. His
other medications included aspirin 81 mg/d, carvedilol phosphate 10
mg/d, candesartan/hydrochlorothiazide 16 mg/12.5 mg daily, and
felodipine 5 mg daily.
When seen in the clinic, he was noted to have a stiff axial
posture with rigid back and thigh musculature. He was awake, alert,
and oriented to time, place, and person. His memory was intact. The
cranial nerves were all intact. He had normal muscle strength, intact
sensory perception, 2 /H11001deep tendon reﬂexes, intact ﬁnger-to-nose
test, but a stiff gait. He had not experienced tremors. The remainder
of the physical examination was found to be normal. Laboratory
studies showed a normal complete blood count and serum chemis-
tries except for a mildly elevated glucose at 140 mg/dL. The
inﬂammatory markers were not elevated, and the creatine kinase was
mildly elevated at 268 IU/L (N: 52–200). The level of aldolase was
normal. ANA titer was 1:320 (mixed pattern) and the SSA antibody

titer was mildly elevated at 51 AU/mL (N: /H1102140). The rest of the
serologic examinations including the following tests: anti-double
stranded deoxyribonucleic acid, extractable nuclear antibody panel,
antiproteinase 3, antimyeloperoxidase, and anti-Jo1, were found to
be negative. C3 and C4 levels were normal. Chest x-ray and
computed tomography scan of the pelvis were normal. The brain
computed tomography scan and MRI were also normal.
Anti-GAD levels were elevated at 102.86 U/mL (radioimmu-
noassay method, N: 0 –1.45 U/mL; ARUP Labs, Salt Lake City,
UT). A diagnosis of SPS was made. Although he had elevated ANA
and SSA antibody titers, he had no other clinical features of systemic
lupus erythematosus, Sjogren syndrome, or any other connective
tissue disease. He was placed on diazepam 10 mg t.i.d. in addition
to baclofen, as a result of which signiﬁcant improvement was seen
in his rigidity. He was later able to ambulate without any assistance.
The prednisone dose was discontinued. However, he complained of
somnolence that signiﬁcantly hindered his ability to function inde-
pendently and also prevented dose optimization. He eventually
received 2 infusions of rituximab 1000 mg 1 week apart. His
condition continued to improve, and he was able to do his daily
activities independently. Post rituximab therapy, the anti-GAD went
down to 89.17 U/mL after 3 months. However, by the fourth month,
it had risen to more than 250 IUva/mL (enzyme-linked immunosor-
bent assay, N: 0 –5.0 IU/mL; ARUP Labs), and was maintained at a
level /H11022250 IU/mL after 6 months (Fig. 1). It should be noted that
although the tests were done in the same laboratory, the methods
used were different. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay is a newer
and simpler method, probably more speciﬁc and sensitive, and the
results obtained using this test correlate well with that of radioim-
munoassay.
8 Both these techniques are reliable, but the methods and
units used by both are different, and therefore it is not possible to
compare and trend the results. Regardless, the anti-GAD level of our
patient remained more than the reportable value (/H11022250 IU/mL), and in
spite of these elevated titers, the patient continued to improve clinically.
The baclofen has been tapered and discontinued, whereas the diazepam
has also been tapered to 10 mg twice a day.
DISCUSSION
SPS is a rare neurologic disorder characterized by progressive
rigidity and muscle spasms. Previous reports indicate diagnosis of
SPS on the basis of clinical criteria including stiffness and rigidity of
the axial muscles, progression to involvement of the proximal limb
muscles, abnormal axial posture with lumbar hyperlordosis, super-
imposed muscle spasms, absence of brainstem, pyramidal, extrapy-
ramidal, and lower motor neuron signs, and absence of cognitive
involvement.
2,9 Although the exact etiology of SPS is unknown, it is
generally considered to be an autoimmune disease in view of the
high prevalence of autoantibodies and associated autoimmune dis-
eases. SPS is characterized by frequently elevated levels of circu-
lating anti-GAD. These antibodies have been shown in vitro to
inhibit the activity of GABA, which is the major inhibitory neuro-
transmitter in the central nervous system. Reduced levels of GABA
in several regions of the brain have been found in patients with
typical SPS.
10 This ﬁnding gives support to the pathologic role of
anti-GAD, and may explain the clinical presentation of SPS. The

impaired inhibitory neurotransmission leads to hyperactivity of the
peripheral motor unit, resulting in rigidity and spasms.
SPS has also been observed in some patients with solid
tumors. This paraneoplastic variant is associated with the presence
of antibodies to amphiphysin, a membrane protein concentrated in
nerve terminals. These patients generally lack anti-GAD, are not
diabetic, and are mostly women with breast cancer.
11
Benzodiazepines are considered the ﬁrst line of treatment for
SPS. These drugs are thought to modulate the activity of GABA.
Diazepam is highly effective in most cases, although sometimes
requiring high doses that may not be tolerated by patients. Baclofen,
another GABA modulating drug, can also be used either as a
monotherapy or in addition with diazepam.
SPS is also highly responsive to immunotherapy, lending
further credence to the autoimmune nature of the disease. The
beneﬁcial effects of these treatments also correlate with the decline
in the anti-GAD titers. Rituximab treatment was also shown to result
in a rapid decline of anti-GAD titers in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid.
7
B cells are a major component of the adaptive immune system
and are produced in the bone marrow. They have multiple diverse
functions, including antibody production, antigen-presentation and
costimulation, release of inﬂammatory and immunomodulatory cy-
tokines (including Interleukin /H20851IL/H20852-10, IL-4, IL-6, lymphotoxin-
/H9251,
transforming growth factor TGF- /H9252, and interferon- /H9253), and possibly
regulate dendritic cell function, and T-helper cell differentiation. 12
Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that reacts with the
CD20 antigen present on all B cells except stem cells, pro-B cells,
and plasma cells.
13 By binding to the CD20 antigen, rituximab
depletes B cells through processes involving antibody-dependent
cellular cytotoxicity, complement-dependent cytotoxicity, and in-
duction of apoptosis. Although B cell depletion has little effect on
circulating T cells, rituximab may indirectly inhibit T cell activation
by inhibiting antigen-presentation by B cells, and reduction in B cell
cytokines. In mouse models of autoimmune arthritis and diabetes, B
cell depletion resulted in inhibition of antigen-speciﬁc CD4
/H11001T cell
activation and expansion. 14 In an open clinical trial in systemic
lupus erythematosus patients with nephritis, rituximab has also been
shown to induce regulatory T cells in patients who were responsive
to the treatment.
15
In the case report by Baker et al, 7 the cerebrospinal ﬂuid
anti-GAD level was undetectable after the ﬁrst rituximab infusion.
The serum anti-GAD levels remained low. However, the patient’s
symptoms reappeared 3 months later which necessitated a repeat
treatment with rituximab. In our case, there was signiﬁcant clinical
improvement after 2 doses of rituximab despite persistence of the
anti-GAD titers, and a repeat treatment was not deemed necessary.

titers went down initially, but subsequent titers remained
highly elevated in spite of continuous clinical improvement.
(Note: the last 2 titers were done at the same laboratory but
using a different method.)

We postulate that the mechanism by which rituximab was associated
with improvement in our patient may involve mechanisms other
than antibody depletion. These may include inhibition of antigen-
presentation and cytokine production of B cells, inhibition of T cell
activation, and induction of regulatory T cells. It is also possible that
the therapeutic effect of rituximab involves depletion of unmeasured
antibodies other than anti-GAD which have yet to be deﬁned.
